questions.stem: A 52-year-old woman has a 3.2-cm purely cystic thyroid nodule found on ultrasound performed for an unrelated reason. She has no compressive symptoms and no cosmetic concerns. Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone is normal, and no suspicious cervical lymph nodes are seen. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Diagnostic fine-needle aspiration, because the nodule exceeds 3 cm

choices.label: B
choices.text: No diagnostic aspiration; drain only for symptoms or cosmesis

choices.label: C
choices.text: Radionuclide thyroid scan to exclude a hyperfunctioning nodule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Thyroid lobectomy to obtain a definitive tissue diagnosis

choices.label: E
choices.text: Radioactive iodine ablation because of the nodule's size

explanation.summary: Purely cystic nodules are a benign-leaning pattern and do not require diagnostic cytology regardless of size.
explanation.whyCorrect: The biopsy threshold follows risk rather than size alone; lower-risk sonographic patterns require larger size before biopsy is even considered, and a purely cystic nodule does not require diagnostic FNA at all. Aspiration of such a cyst is done for symptomatic or cosmetic reasons, not to obtain a diagnosis. A larger purely cystic nodule can be less concerning than a small solid hypoechoic one with irregular margins.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Size alone does not trigger biopsy when the sonographic pattern is purely cystic.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Radionuclide scanning follows a low TSH, and this patient's TSH is normal.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surgery is not indicated for an asymptomatic benign-appearing cystic lesion.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Radioiodine treats selected functional thyroid disorders, not a normal-TSH cystic nodule.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a normal serum thyroid-stimulating hormone undergoes ultrasound of a 1.9-cm thyroid nodule. Which of the following sonographic findings is most reassuring?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Spongiform composition with smooth margins

choices.label: B
choices.text: Solid, very hypoechoic composition

choices.label: C
choices.text: Irregular, infiltrative margins

choices.label: D
choices.text: Taller-than-wide shape on transverse imaging

choices.label: E
choices.text: Punctate echogenic foci within the nodule

explanation.summary: Spongiform architecture and smooth margins are benign-leaning ultrasound features.
explanation.whyCorrect: Benign-leaning findings include purely cystic or spongiform composition, smooth margins, comet-tail artifact, and a wider-than-tall shape. A spongiform nodule is a very-low-suspicion pattern for which observation is often reasonable in the absence of suspicious lymph nodes. Higher-risk patterns, by contrast, lower the size threshold for biopsy.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Solid, very hypoechoic composition is one of the core suspicious features.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Irregular or infiltrative margins are a suspicious feature.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Taller-than-wide shape is suspicious; wider-than-tall is the reassuring orientation.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Punctate echogenic foci are a suspicious finding, unlike comet-tail artifact.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old man presents with an anterior neck mass that has enlarged rapidly over four weeks. The mass is hard and fixed to underlying tissue. He has new hoarseness, dysphagia, and exertional dyspnea. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Papillary thyroid carcinoma

choices.label: B
choices.text: Follicular thyroid carcinoma

choices.label: C
choices.text: Medullary thyroid carcinoma

choices.label: D
choices.text: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma

choices.label: E
choices.text: Benign colloid nodule

explanation.summary: Rapid neck enlargement with local invasive symptoms is the classic presentation of anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.
explanation.whyCorrect: Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is highly aggressive and may present with rapid neck enlargement, local invasion, hoarseness, dysphagia, dyspnea, and a poor prognosis. Rapid growth, a fixed or hard mass, hoarseness, and dysphagia or dyspnea are all red flags in thyroid nodule evaluation, and here they cluster together over weeks. That tempo and degree of local invasion is not typical of the differentiated thyroid cancers.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Papillary carcinoma usually presents as a thyroid nodule with possible cervical nodal spread, not fulminant local invasion.
whyWrongByChoice.B: Follicular carcinoma is defined by capsular and vascular invasion and spreads hematogenously to lung and bone.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Medullary carcinoma arises from C cells and is suggested by calcitonin production or a MEN2 family history.
whyWrongByChoice.E: A benign colloid nodule does not grow rapidly, become fixed, or cause hoarseness and stridor.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old woman undergoes diagnostic lobectomy for a follicular-pattern thyroid nodule. Histologic examination shows tumor penetrating the capsule and invading vessels within the capsule. Which of the following patterns of metastatic spread is most characteristic of this tumor?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Hematogenous spread to lung and bone

choices.label: B
choices.text: Lymphatic spread to cervical lymph nodes

choices.label: C
choices.text: Direct invasion of trachea and larynx within weeks

choices.label: D
choices.text: Peritoneal seeding to intra-abdominal organs

choices.label: E
choices.text: Spread limited to within the thyroid capsule

explanation.summary: Follicular thyroid carcinoma, defined by capsular and vascular invasion, disseminates through the bloodstream.
explanation.whyCorrect: Capsular and/or vascular invasion is the defining feature of follicular thyroid carcinoma, which is why the lobectomy was needed to make the diagnosis. Tumor entry into vessels within the capsule is the anatomic basis for its behavior. Follicular carcinoma tends to spread hematogenously, especially to lung and bone.

whyWrongByChoice.B: Cervical nodal spread is characteristic of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Rapid local invasion of airway structures characterizes anaplastic carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Peritoneal seeding is not a described route of spread for thyroid carcinoma.
whyWrongByChoice.E: The demonstrated capsular and vascular invasion is precisely what makes this tumor capable of distant spread.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man has a 2.2-cm thyroid nodule and a suppressed serum thyroid-stimulating hormone. Radionuclide scanning shows decreased uptake in the nodule compared with the surrounding thyroid tissue. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Proceed to total thyroidectomy, since cold nodules are malignant

choices.label: B
choices.text: Ultrasound risk stratification, with FNA if criteria are met

choices.label: C
choices.text: No further evaluation, since cold nodules are usually benign

choices.label: D
choices.text: Radioactive iodine therapy directed at the hypofunctioning nodule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Levothyroxine suppression with a repeat scan in six months

explanation.summary: A cold nodule is neither dismissed nor assumed malignant; it re-enters the ultrasound-based pathway.
explanation.whyCorrect: A nonfunctioning nodule shows decreased uptake relative to surrounding thyroid tissue, which answers the functional question but not the structural one. Cold nodules are not automatically malignant, so the workup returns to ultrasound risk stratification. Fine-needle aspiration follows only when nodule size, sonographic pattern, lymph-node findings, and clinical context meet criteria.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Cold uptake does not establish malignancy and does not by itself justify thyroidectomy.
whyWrongByChoice.C: Stopping here skips the structural assessment that determines whether biopsy is needed.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Radioiodine treats hyperfunctioning thyroid tissue; a cold nodule would not concentrate it.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Suppression and a repeat scan neither characterize the nodule structurally nor obtain tissue.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old woman with a multinodular goiter has a suppressed serum thyroid-stimulating hormone. Radionuclide scanning shows focal increased uptake in a 2.5-cm right-lobe nodule. Ultrasound additionally shows a 1.5-cm solid hypoechoic left-lobe nodule with irregular margins and punctate echogenic foci. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

choices.label: A
choices.text: No biopsy, since the hot nodule explains the suppressed TSH

choices.label: B
choices.text: Fine-needle aspiration of the suspicious left-lobe nodule

choices.label: C
choices.text: Fine-needle aspiration of the hyperfunctioning right-lobe nodule

choices.label: D
choices.text: Total thyroidectomy without further assessment of either nodule

choices.label: E
choices.text: Repeat radionuclide scanning in six months before any biopsy

explanation.summary: In multinodular disease, a hot nodule explains the low TSH but does not clear the other nodules.
explanation.whyCorrect: One hyperfunctioning nodule can account for a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone, yet other nonfunctioning or suspicious nodules still require ultrasound-based assessment. The left-lobe lesion is solid and hypoechoic with irregular margins and punctate echogenic foci, a suspicious pattern that carries a low size threshold for biopsy. It should be aspirated while the hormone excess from the hot nodule is managed separately.

whyWrongByChoice.A: Explaining the low TSH does not settle the structural risk of a separate, sonographically suspicious nodule.
whyWrongByChoice.C: The hyperfunctioning nodule is usually lower risk for malignancy and does not typically require FNA.
whyWrongByChoice.D: Surgery is premature before the suspicious nodule has been characterized cytologically.
whyWrongByChoice.E: Delaying six months leaves a nodule that already meets criteria for tissue sampling unevaluated.
